reference:
Bàbá àgbàlagbà kan ni wọ́n wá sí ilé ìwòsàn alábòde wa. Bàbá yìí sọ pé orí ń fò ó gan-an, ọrùn rẹ̀ sì le, ó sì ní kokoro kan ní ojijì tí ó sú sí i ní ara. Ó wá láti béèrè ohun tí ó lè fà á àti irú ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún un.
A béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá yìí pé ṣé orí náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì ni tàbí pé ó ti ń fò ó díẹ̀díẹ̀. Bàbá náà sì sọ pé lójijì ni ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ ní òru, ó sì ti lágbára gan-an báyìí. A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé ṣé ó lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ dáadáa, bàbá náà sì sọ pé rárá, kò lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ nítorí pé ó máa ń wọ agbárí rẹ̀, tí orí náà sì tún máa ń fò ó sí i.
A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé kokoro tí ó ń mú un yìí, ṣé ó ń le tàbí ó pọ̀, tàbí pé ó fẹ́rẹ̀fẹ́ ni. Bàbá náà sọ pé gbogbo ara òun ni, kò sì lè mọ ibi pàtó, ṣùgbọ́n ó ń yún un.
Lẹ́yìn náà, a béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá náà pé ṣé ó ní ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan láìpẹ́ yìí, bàbá náà sì sọ pé wọn kò lọ sí ibi kankan ju pé wọ́n tà ọjà ní iwájú ilé wọn. Wọ́n kò sì ní ìfarakànra pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan.
Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà ni pé kí ni ó lè fà irú àìsàn orífífó àti ọrùn líle tí bàbá yìí kò lè yí ọrùn rẹ̀, tí kokoro sì bò ó ní gbogbo ara? Kí ló lè fà á? Ṣé àrùn ẹyí ni èyí tàbí nǹkan míì?
Ìbéèrè wa kejì ni pé irú àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí ṣe láti mọ ohun tí ń ṣe é ní pàtó fún ìtọ́jú tó péye, àti pé oogun wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí lò kí èsì àyẹ̀wò rẹ̀ tó dé?
model_answer: Àmì àìsàn bíi orí fífọ́ jẹ́, orùn líle, àti àìlẹ́wọ́ wo ina mọ́lẹ̀ fi hàn pé ó ṣeé jẹ́ àrùn kòkòrò inú ọpọlọ bíi Meningitis tàbí Cerebral malaria (Peye), nígbà tí ìrírí kòkòrò lójìí jẹ́ ẹ̀rín ìrònú (hallucination) tí gbigbona àrùn inú ń fa. Àrùn yìí jẹ́ kíkankíkan tó le pa láìsì ìtọ́jú gidi, nítorí náà kò sí ògùn ilẹ̀ mìíràn yàtọ̀ sí Paracetamol àti ogun Pẹ̀yẹ (antimalarial) tí a lè fún un lásìkò títí a fi ń gbé e lọ sí ìwòsàn. Ìtọ́jú tó yẹ ni kí a lọsẹ̀sẹ̀ gbé e lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn fún ayẹwo ẹ̀jẹ̀ kí Dókítà lè bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìtọ́jú gidi bíi ogun àjẹsẹ́ra (antibiotics) pẹ̀lú ọwọ́ ẹ̀jẹ̀ láììdalẹ́dàà.

question: Ìyàwó kan lori wipe oko re wupọ gan ni gbogbo aarọ nigba ji lori ibusun ikona ma n bẹrẹ lẹsẹkẹsẹ o si maa n gba akoko lati dawo duro bi ọjọ ṣe n lo o tu ri pe oko re n tiraka lati mi dada nigbamii bi o ba rin jinna diẹ tabi gun atẹgun o maa n duro. láti gba ìmí rẹ̀ padà ó tún máa rẹ́ kíákíá ní alẹ́ ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ lo ìgbà pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́ ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ronú bóyá àrùn kan wà lẹ́ tí ó ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. reference:
Ìyàwó kan rí i pé ọkọ rẹ̀ ń wúkọ́ gan-an nígbà tí wọ́n bá jí ní orí ibùsùn. Ikọ́ náà máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì, ó sì máa ń gba àkókò kí ó tó dáwọ́ dúró. Bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ó tún ń rí i pé ọkọ rẹ̀ ń tiraka láti mí dáadáa. Nígbà tí ó bá rìn jìnnà díẹ̀ tàbí gùn àtẹ̀gùn, ó máa ń dúró láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà, ó tún máa ń rẹ̀ kíákíá.
Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ gba àkókò pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà, inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́. Ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í rò pé bóyá àrùn kan wà tí ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó bá ọkọ rẹ̀ sọ̀rọ̀ pé kí wọ́n lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, kí wọ́n lè rí dókítà, kí wọ́n lè mọ ohun tí ń ṣẹlẹ̀ gan-an.
Ìbéèrè ni pé kí ni ó lè fà kí ikọ́ ní agbára tó bẹ́ẹ̀, kí ara ẹni máa rẹ̀ ní gbogbo ìgbà, kí ènìyàn tún ní ìṣòro mímí dáadáa nígbà gbogbo tí ikọ́ bá ń wáyé? Ṣé ìṣòro yìí lè ní ṣe pẹ̀lú àrùn ẹdọforo tàbí àrùn ọkàn nìkan? Kí ni àwọn ohun tí ó lè mú ikú wá, kí ó sì jẹ́ kí ènìyàn máa tiraka láti mí, tí ó sì lewu débi pé ènìyàn gbọ́dọ̀ tètè lọ ṣàyẹ̀wò?
Kí ni àwọn àmi ewu mímí tí ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀ máa ṣọ́ra fún nípa ikọ́ àti ìṣòro mímí?
model_answer: Àrùn ọkàn (heart failure) tàbí àrùn ẹ̀dọ̀fóró gẹ́gẹ́ bíi asima (asthma) tàbí ẹ̀dọ̀fóró ríro (COPD/Tuberculosis) ni ó wọ́pọ̀ jùlọ tí ó ń fa ìkọ́ àárọ̀ kíákíá àti tiraka láti mí nígbà ìṣẹ́ àti ní alẹ́. Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni, àrùn ọkàn àti ẹ̀dọ̀fóró ni wọ́n ń fa àwọn ìṣòro wọ̀nyí jù, ṣùgbọ́n àrùn míràn bíi àìní ẹ̀jẹ̀ pọ̀ (anemia) lè ṣàkóbá àrùn ọkàn náà pẹ̀lú. Àmì ewu tí wọ́n yẹ kí ẹ ṣọ́ fún ni: bí ó bá ń tiraka láti mí rárá rárá bí ó tilẹ̀ jọwọ́, kò lè sọ̀rọ̀ àjẹmọ́ta, ẹ̀ẹ́mú rẹ̀ ń yọ kò bóòró (cyanosis), tàbí kí ó jẹ̀yìn ikọ́ èjè. Ó ṣe pàtàkì kí ẹ yàrà lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn fún àyẹ̀wò bíi X-ray ẹ̀dọ̀fóró àti ECG ọkàn lónìí láti mọ kòròáyà rẹ̀. Kí ẹ má ṣe lo ogun aláṣẹyọ̀ tàbí ogun ìbílẹ̀ funra yín nínú ìṣòro yìí, ẹ yàrà bá dókítà fún itọ́ju tó yẹ kí e má bàa dàrú lójú.

question: Ọ̀kan lára àwọn olóyún wa la rí ní àfẹ̀mọjúmọ̀ yìí pẹ̀lú ọkọ̀ wọn, wọ́n sọ wípé àwọn ní ìrora tí ó lágbára ni inú àwọn tí ẹ̀yin sì ń rú àwọn tí kò sì tí tó ọjọ́ ìbí àwọn abìnrin wabìnrin pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀ a tún wá bẹ̀ wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ohun ò ń fi wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ nígbà náà ni abo arabìnrin. wí pé njẹ wọn rí omi àbí ẹ̀jẹ̀ san sọ wípé àmúrí omi amọ sì rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ àtúnwá bèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọkeló ní oyún ti wọn ni wọn oyún eleke lo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú tó ń sọ wípé oyún alákọ́èrè wa fún dókítà wa ní wípé mi lè jẹ́ lè tọ́ka sí ààmí ìrọ̀bí àbí àmì wípé oyún bájìn mìíràn ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ? arábìnrin yẹn lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú, ilé ìta ń pè ní san láti mú nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀.

A béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ó mú wọn, ó ń fi wọ́n sílẹ̀, wọ́n sì ní àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. Nígbà náà ni a béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n rí omi àbí rí ẹ̀jẹ̀, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn rí omi àti ẹ̀jẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọ ẹlẹ́kẹlo, oyún ẹlẹ́kẹlo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú wọn, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún àlá kọ kọ́. Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà wa ni pé ǹjẹ́ àmì yìí lè tọ́ka sí àmì ìrọbí àbí àmì wípé oyún bàjẹ́ àbí àmì míràn? Ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ wípé kí arábìnrin yìí lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú rẹ̀ tí a ń pè ní <codeswitch> <English> scan láti mọ nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀?
model_answer: Kì í ṣe oyún alákọ́èrè (ectopic pregnancy) nítorí pé oyún bẹ́ẹ̀ máa ń fọ́ ní ọ̀sẹ̀ mẹ́fà sí mẹ́wàá, kì í ṣeé gbé dé ọṣù mẹ́fà. Àwọn ààmí rẹ̀ bíi ìrora inú ibàjí, ìrú omi àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ fihan ìpọ́njú oyún tó lágbára gẹ́gẹ́ bíi kíkọ́júde agbárá-omi oyún (PPROM), yíyọ placenta (abruption), tàbí bímọ lọ́wọ́ kí ọjọ́ ìbí tó (preterm labor). Bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ wípé ó ti lọ ṣe fọ́tò inú (ultrasound), ó pọn dandan kí wọ́n gbé e wá ilé ìwòsàn láìpẹ́ fún ìyẹ̀wò àdánù àti ìtọ́jú dókítà aláboyún lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. Ìdálọ́wọ́dúró láti fi ìyẹ̀wò ìdájìì lẹ́sẹ̀kẹ́sẹ̀ lè fa ìpalára tàbí ikú fún ọmọ oyún náà nítorí pé kò tíì tó ọjọ́ ìbí àti pé ó jẹ́ oyún àkọ́kọ́ rẹ̀. Nítorí ìdí èyí, kí wọ́n má bẹ̀ẹ́ fi ìtọ́jú ilé ìwòsàn ṣeré, kí wọ́n sì tẹ̀lé ìmọ̀ràn dókítà láti dẹ́kùn wíwọ́nàọ́nà míràn.

question: Dókítà ìyẹ ọmọkùnrin tó ń gbé ní ilé wa ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ṣe àkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ̀ kò mọ ọmú dáadáa ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún ní ọmọ náà máa mú díẹ̀ lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ́ ọmọ náà tóbi pé ọmọ náà ò ní agbára láti mu ọmú ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀ kì í ṣe èyí. nìkan èmi rẹ̀ ó yí padà o máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mi lọ sókè o ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀ bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ ìyá ọmọ náà túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù ó ń wò bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà ò jẹ́ ohun tó ni àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èyí àti bó ṣe ń láàgùn nítorí náà ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láti rí dókítà fún. wò ọmọ náà ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fàá kí ọmọ máa ń ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa náà ṣe mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún ló lè fa? Bí ọmọdé máa làágùn nígbà tó bá ń mu omú.
reference:
Dokita, iya ọmọ kan tó ń gbé ní ilé wa, ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ kò mu ọmú dáadáa. Ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún un ní ọmú, ọmọ náà máa mu díẹ̀, lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ̀ẹ́. Ìyá ọmọ náà tún rí pé ọmọ náà kò ní agbára láti mu ọmú, ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀. Kì í ṣe èyí nìkan, èémí rẹ̀ ó yí padà, ó máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mí lọ sókè, ó ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀, bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí. Bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ìyá ọmọ náà ń túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù, ó ń wo bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà kò jẹun tó ni, àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èémí àti bóyá ṣe ń làágùn. Nítorí náà, ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Láti rí dókítà fún àyẹ̀wò ọmọ náà. Ìbéèrè mi ni wípé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa? Ṣé bí ọmọ náà ṣe ń mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún? Kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ kékeré máa làágùn nígbà tí ó bá ń mu ọmú?
English Translation
model_answer: Àìléwà mu ọmú dáadáa àti láágùn jẹ́ àwọn ìkìlọ̀ ọ̀gọ́rọ̀-ìn (danger signs) tó ń fàá nítorí àrùn ẹ̀yà mímí bíi aáwọ̀ ẹ̀yà (pneumonia) tàbí àrùn jẹjẹrẹ inú (sepsis). Nígbà tí ọmọdé ń láágùn, kò ní agbára láti mu ọmú dáadáa nítorí pé ó ń fi gbogbo agbára rẹ̀ ṣe iṣẹ́ mímí, èyí sì máa ń fa kí ó dáwọ́ dúró láìpẹ́ láti lè mí. Ní àwọn àgbègbè wa, irúfẹ́ ìṣòro báyìí ti wọ́pọ̀ láàárín àwọn ọmọdé, ó sì lè wá nítorí kòkòrò àrùn tàbí nígbà mìíràn àrùn ọkàn. Ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe ohun tó yẹ nípasẹ̀ bíbí gbé e lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, àyẹ̀wò sì yóò ṣe ìmúṣẹ àdánwò láti mọ kókó tó ń fa àrùn náà. Kí ìyá náà má fún ọmọ náà ní ògùn ilẹ̀kùn yálà nílé, kí ó sì jẹ́ kí dókítà bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìtọ́jú pẹ̀lú fífínín omi-afẹ́fẹ́ (oxygen) àti ògùn àjẹjẹrẹ (antibiotics) bí ó ti yẹ.

question: ọmọ kan yóò ṣàkíyèsí fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí ọmọ yẹn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní wúkọ́ láì dáwọ́ dúró ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀ kúrò pé òtútù lóko sọmọ náà láyà pé ó máa lọ ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù ní gbogbo alẹ́ ọmọ náà máa jí nílòji nítorí ikọ́ nígbà mi ó máa ń wù wá bẹ́ẹ̀ ni pé ó ṣò. Gbogbo fún láti lè mí dáadáa máa gbé sókè ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tó bá mú èyí ń mu kí ọmọ náà máa lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́ ní ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà tó wúkọ́ gan tó sì tiraka láti lè mí dáadáa ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí. Ilé ìwòsàn ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa iko náà àti ìṣòro tó fi ń tó fa láti mí dáadáa àti bí ó ṣe lè rán ọmọ náà lọ́wọ́ béèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa wuko gan kò sì ní ìṣòro láti lè mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́ kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra? Fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ́ àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ yìí?
reference:
Ìyá ọmọ kan ló ṣàkíyèsí wípé fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí, pé ọmọ òun bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í wúkọ láì dáwọ́ dúró. Ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀, ó rò pé òtútù ló kọ ọmọ náà láyà, pé ó máa lọ. Ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù. Ní gbogbo alẹ́, ọmọ náà máa jí lójijì nítorí ikọ́. Nígbà míì, ó máa ń wíwá bí ẹni pé ó ṣòro fún un láti mí dáadáa. Ìyá rẹ̀ máa gbé e sókè, ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tí ó bá ń mí. Èyí mú kí ọmọ náà má lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́.
Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà ti wúkọ gan-an tí ó sì tiraka láti mí dáadáa, ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa ikọ́ náà àti ìṣòro tó fa láti má lè mí dáadáa, àti bí ó ṣe lè ràn án lọ́wọ́.
Ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ máa wúkọ gan, kí ó sì ní ìṣòro láti mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí ó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ? Àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ́ yìí?
model_answer: Ọwọ́n àdánwò àti ọmọ náà kíkọ́ tí kò dínkù ló ma ń fa àìlèèmí, èyí sábàá máa ń ṣẹlẹ̀ nítorí àrùn bi pneumonia (ogun ẹ̀fọ́rí), bronchiolitis, tàbí asthma, tí ó máa ń burú nítorí òtútù ní alẹ́. Àwọn àmì ẹ̀kún ewu tí wọ́n yẹ kí ìyá máa ṣọ́ra fún ni mí kíákíá, ayà rí kíkankíkan tàbí fífẹ́ gẹ́gẹ́ bíi ṣíṣẹ́ (chest in-drawing), yíyọ ẹ̀fọ́nú, àti ayọ́jẹ́ tàbí àìlèjẹ. Láti dènà àìsàn yìí, ẹ gbọdọ̀ yàgò fún ẹ̀fínnì (smoke) bíi iná kíkún sísun tàbí siga, yíyọ omo náà han òtútù lọ́wọ́, àti afẹ́fẹ̀ àjálẹ̀ (dust) tó lè ko àrùn wá. Ẹ rí dájú pé ibùgbé ọmọ náà gbóná, kí ó sì tẹ́ẹ́rín láti jẹ́ kí afẹ́fẹ̀ tọrọ, kí ẹ sì rí i dájú pé omo náà ń gba abẹ́rẹ̀ ìdènà àjẹsára tó yẹ. Nítorí pé àrùn yìí lè yí padà dé ẹ̀kún ewú lásìkò yìí, ó pọn dandan kí wọ́n gbé ọmọ náà lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láìbánujẹ́ fún ìtọ́jú tó yẹ.

question: Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdún mẹ́sàn ni mo gbé wá sí ilé ìwòsàn ní ọ̀sán yìí mo ná ọmọ náà níṣẹ́ láti ra nǹkan fún mi ní ìgboro ṣùgbọ́n a já bu ọmọ náà jẹ nígbà tí wọ́n mú ọmọ náà délé tí wọ́n sì ṣàlàyé fún mi tó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ náà mo wo ojú egbò tí ajá ti bu ọmọ náà jẹ mo rí pé ojú egbò náà pọ́n ó sì ti wú a ṣe ìwádìí ládùgbò láti mor tó ọmọ náà jẹ́ olówó ajá náà sì sọ wípé àwọn kò gba abere fún ajá náà rí pé lẹ́yìn kí ó jáde kó ṣeré kó sì padà wọlé, wọ́n ní àwọn ogbà ìtọ́jú kankan fún ajá náà rì ni ẹ̀rù ṣe bà mí láti gbé ọmọ náà wá sí ilé ìwòsàn kó má jẹ́ wípé ajá tó bu ọmọ náà jẹ́ ó jẹ́ ajá digbolugi Kí ló ṣeéṣe kó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ tí a já bùjẹ? Kí ló ṣeéṣe kí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ojú egbò tí ó ń pọ́n tí ó sì ń wú? N ó ṣe kí ẹran ipá tí ẹ ti wọnú egbò yìí ó ṣe kí ọmọ náà kó kí nǹkan kó ṣe ọmọ. Ọmọ náà látàrí ọmọ tí a já wo ni mo lè ṣe láti má jẹ́ kí ẹran ipa wọnú egbò yìí awọn abẹ́rẹ́ wo àwọn oògùn a lè fi tọ́jú ọmọdé yìí láti jẹ́ kó ní ìtọ́jú tó péye. Àwọn ohun wo ni a tún lè ṣe tàbí ayewo lale ṣe láti tọju oju egbo ti a ja ti ọmọde.
reference:
Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdun mẹsan ni mo gbe wa si ile-iwosan ni ọsan yi. Mo ran ọmọ naa ni iṣẹ lati ra nkan fun mi ni igboro, ṣugbọn aja bu ọmọ naa jẹ. Nigba ti wọn mu ọmọ naa dele, ti wọn si ṣalaye fun mi ohun to ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ naa, mo wo oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọ naa jẹ, mo ri pe oju egbo naa pọn, o si ti wú. A ṣe iwadi ni adugbo lati mọ irú aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, olowo aja naa si sọ wipe awọn kò gba abẹrẹ fun aja naa rí, wipe lẹyin ki o jade, ko ṣere, ko si pada wọle. Wọn ni awọn o gba itọju kankan fun aja naa rí. Idi eyi ni ẹru ṣe bami lati gbe ọmọ naa wa si ile-iwosan, ko ma jẹ wipe aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, o jẹ aja digbolugi. Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ yi? Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si oju egbo ti o n pọn, ti o si n wú? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ẹran ipa ti ẹ ti wọnu egbo yi? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ọmọ naa... ki nkan ko ṣe ọmọ naa latari ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ? Ẹ jọọ...
Awọn wo ni mo le ṣe lati ma jẹ ki ẹran ipa wọnu egbo yi? Awọn abẹrẹ wo, awọn ogun wo ni a le fi tọju ọmọde yi lati jẹ ko ni itọju to peye? Awọn wo ni a tun le ṣe tabi ayẹwo wo la le ṣe lati tọju oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọde yi jẹ?
model_answer: Ojú egbò tí ó ń pọ́n àti ń wú túmọ̀ sí wípé kòkòrò (bacteria) bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í jẹ ojú egbò náà nítorí ìjẹ ajá, àti nítorí pé ajá náà kò gba àbẹ́rẹ́ ẹran-ibà (rabies), ọmọ náà wà nínú ewu ńlá lórí àrùn ẹran-ibà tó le pa á. Kí ẹ fi omi àti oṣẹ yọ ojú egbò náà kíkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹ́sẹ̀ kí ẹ sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ ìmú ọ̀gùn agbóguntọ̀kọ (antibiotics) àti àbẹ́rẹ́ tetanus láti dẹ́kùn àrùn kòkòrò náà. Láti dẹ́kùn ẹran-ibà, ọmọ náà gbọdọ̀ gba àbẹ́rẹ́ ajẹsára ẹran-ibà (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis) láìṣe ìdààmú, nítorí pé kò sí ìwòsàn fún ẹran-ibà nígbà tí ó bá ti bẹ̀rẹ̀. Kí ẹ tún máa ṣàyẹ̀wò ojú egbò náà láti rí i dájú pé kò wú búburú tàbí kí ẹran rẹ̀ kóò ma wù, kí ẹ sì tọ́jú ajá náà tàbí kí ẹ pa á láti lè ṣàyẹ̀wò ọpọlọ rẹ̀ fún àrùn náà. Bí ó tilẹ̀ jẹ́ pé àwọn ìgbésẹ̀ ìdẹ̀kùn wọ̀nyí ṣe pàtàkì, ẹ gbọdọ̀ gbé ọmọ náà wá sí ilé ìwòsàn báyìí fún ìtọ́jú ọ̀gùn àti àbẹ́rẹ́ tó péye lábẹ́ ìmọ̀sáyẹ́nsí.

question: Alágbà tó ṣàkíyèsí wípé ọmọ náà ń wúkọ́ gidigidi débi pé ó ń ta gì pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa wúkó àtarìbi wí pé kò lè mí dáadáa tó ń tiraka láti mi irú ni a lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún Bákan náà irú ìmọ̀ràn wo ni a lè gba ìyá ọ lágbà ìtọ́jú ọmọdé náà?
reference: Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ kan ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ náà wúkọ́ gidigidi, dé bi pé òun tàgìrì àti wí pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni. Kí ó le fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa n wúkọ́ àwú tagìrì, débi wípé kò le mí dáadáa, tó tiraka láti mí? Irú àyẹ̀wò wo la lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà? Irú ìtọ́jú wo la lè fún? Bákan náà irú àmọ̀rà wo la lè gba Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ náà?
model_answer: Kíkọ́-mí-i tó ń yá àti títà gì fún ọmọdé ni ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀ nítorí ìdààmú àrùn àtarìbi (asthma), èyí tí kòkòrò inú afẹ́fẹ́, yíyí tutù, tàbí eéfín ń fa kí ọ̀nà èémí rẹ kí ó dín kù. Ìtọ́jú tó yẹ ni kí a fún ọmọ náà ní òórùn (oxygen) nítorí pé ó ń tiraka, kí a sì fún un ní egbògi àbọ̀-èémí gẹ́gẹ́ bí Salbutamol àti egbògi àkóbá gẹ́gẹ́ bí Prednisolone láti fún ọ̀nà èémí rẹ̀ sí taara. Mo ṣè ìmọ̀ràn fún ìyá náà kí ó dá àwọn nkan tó ń fa àrùn náà mọ́ gẹ́gẹ́ bí eéfín iná, yíyí tutù, àti òróró-lẹ̀rẹ̀, kí ó sì máa bá ọmọ náà wà ní àyè tó gbóná. Kí ìyá náà máa lò egbògi ìdènà àti ti ìmúlò fún àrùn náà lásìkò tó péye gẹ́gẹ́ bí a ti kọ̀sínà, kí ó sì máa mu un wá àyẹ̀wò lọ́dọ̀ dókítà ní ìgbàkì-gbà. Nítorí pé ìdààmú èémí tó ń ta gì wà nínú ewu, ó ṣe pàtàkì kí a gbé ọmọ náà wá ilé ìwòsàn lọ́wọ́ lọ́wọ́ fún ìtọ́jú àgbáyanú kí a má báà sọ ọ́ di aláìsí.

question: Arabinrin ọmọ ogbon odun lo bimọ bi iṣẹju merinlelogbon seyin a sọ pe bi ṣe rọrun nigba ti arabinrin yii bi ọmọ rẹ omo naa n sun ju o nira fun gan lati ke ko si ṣe daada ọmọ naa ko sunkun pupọ lẹsẹkẹsẹ nigbati a bi tan o si dabi ẹni pe o nira fun lati ji Àwọ̀ ara rẹ̀ dá bí ẹni pé ó fẹ́ sán kò gbé apá rẹ̀ àti ẹsẹ̀ rẹ̀ dáadáa bó ṣe yẹ kó gbún lè jẹun torí wípé ó ń sùn jù kò sì lè fa ọmú dáadáa ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe àníyàn wípé àwọn ọmọ òun tó bí tẹ́lẹ̀ kété tí òun bá bí wọn tán, wọ́n máa ń sunkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ yìí? reference:
Arábìnrin kan, ẹni ọdún ọgbọ̀n, ló bímọ ní ìṣẹ́jú díẹ̀ sẹ́yìn. A sọ pé ìbímọ náà lọ dáadáa. Ṣùgbọ́n láti ìgbà tí a bí ọmọ náà, ọmọ náà ń ṣòro gan-an. Kò ń sunkún dáadáa, kò sì ń dáhùn bí ọmọ tuntun ṣe yẹ.
Lẹ́yìn ìbí, ọmọ náà kò súnkún dáadáa, ó sì dà bí ẹni pé ó ní ìṣòro láti jí. Ara rẹ̀ dá bí ẹni pé kò rọrùn, ọwọ́ àti ẹsẹ̀ rẹ̀ kò ń rìn dáadáa bí ó ṣe yẹ. Kò tún lè jẹun dáadáa, ó sì ń ṣòro fún un láti fà ọmú.
Ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe àníyàn torí pé àwọn ọmọ rẹ̀ tó ti bí tẹ́lẹ̀ máa ń sunkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbí. Kí ni ó lè fà ìṣòro yìí? Àwọn àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ṣe lórí ọmọ náà, àti kí ni ìgbésẹ̀ pajawiri tí a lè gbé? Kí ni a lè ṣe fún ọmọ kékeré yìí?
model_answer: Àwọn àmì tí ọmọ náà ń fìhàn tàbí ṣeṣe lórí ìdààmú ẹ̀mí nígbà ìbímọ́ (birth asphyxia), àìtó súgà nínú ẹ̀jẹ̀ (hypoglycemia), tàbí ipa oògùn ìyàsùn tàbí ìdàrò tí ìyá rẹ̀ lè gbà lákòókò ìbímọ́. Àwọn àyẹ̀wò pàtàkì ni kí a yẹ ìgbóná ara rẹ̀, ṣàyẹ̀wò súgà inú ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀, yẹ àwọn àmì ẹ̀mí (APGAR score) kí a tún yọ̀wọ́ ìtàn oògùn ìyá náà. Ìgbésẹ̀ ìpajárì tó yá ni kí a gbé ọmọ náà sí abẹ́ ojú-ọwọ́ ìgbóná (radiant warmer), kí a ṣèrànwọ́ fún ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ bí ó ti yẹ, kí a sì máa mú ọmọ náà dùn kí ó máa sun mọ́. Nítorí pé ó ń sùn ju kò sì le fa ọmú, a gbọ́dọ̀ fi omi ọmú tí a yọ lọ́wọ́ ìyá fún un tàbí kí a fi ọmú tẹ̀ẹ́ fún un láti dẹ́kùn kí eégún inú rẹ̀ kó má bàa jẹ, tàbí kí a fún ní oògùn ìwọ̀n suga inú wẹ́wẹ́ (IV dextrose) tí ó bá wọ́pọ̀. Àyẹ̀wọ̀ tí ó yẹ kí ó ṣe ni: àyẹ̀wò ẹ̀jẹ̀ (blood test), àyẹ̀wò omi ọpọlọ (CSF analysis/lumbar puncture), àti àyẹ̀wò tipínmá (malaria parasite). model_answer:
A hard breast lump can be caused by many things, including a benign fibroadenoma, breast cyst, infection/abscess, fat necrosis after injury, hormonal breast changes, or breast cancer.  
Not every breast lump is cancer, but any **new, hard, painless, or persistent lump** should be checked promptly because early breast cancer can also present that way.  
She should see a doctor for proper breast examination and usually a breast ultrasound or mammogram, and if needed FNAC/core biopsy to know exactly what it is.  
Other warning signs include nipple discharge especially blood, nipple turning inward, change in breast size/shape, skin dimpling or “orange-peel” skin, redness/swelling, sores on the breast, lump in the armpit, or persistent unexplained breast pain.  
She should not rely on herbs or massage; early hospital assessment gives the best chance of cure if it is serious.

This is an emergency: yellow eyes/skin with high fever, chills, severe headache, vomiting and not eating can be severe malaria with jaundice, acute hepatitis, sepsis, sickle-cell/haemolysis, or another serious liver/blood infection.  
Please take them to the emergency unit now for vital signs and tests: malaria test/film, full blood count/PCV, blood sugar, liver function and bilirubin, kidney/electrolytes, urine test, and hepatitis screening.  
They may need admission for IV fluids, anti-vomiting medicine, fever control, and urgent treatment such as IV artesunate for severe malaria or antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
Do not continue herbal mixtures or excess paracetamol, as these can worsen liver injury; bring all medicines already given and any sickle-cell history/vaccination history.  
If they are weak, confused, very drowsy, passing dark urine, not urinating, or convulsing, treat it as life-threatening and seek help immediately.

A thirty-three-year-old pregnant woman who is seven months pregnant was brought to our hospital by her neighbors. They explained that she suddenly developed severe abdominal pain, and a large amount of blood began to come out from her vagina. Her body was shaking, and she was crying because the pain was intense. Their third question was: What investigations or tests can be carried out?
Their fourth question was: What treatment is appropriate for her condition?
Their fifth question was: What foods should this pregnant woman avoid, and what hygiene measures should she observe?
model_answer:
The most likely cause is **placental abruption**—the placenta separates before delivery, causing **severe abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, uterine tightening/shaking and danger to mother and baby**; placenta praevia or uterine rupture are other emergencies to rule out.  

She needs **immediate emergency care**: call obstetric/surgical team, put her on the left side, give oxygen, insert 2 large IV lines, start fluids, check vital signs and fetal heartbeat, take blood for urgent cross‑match, prepare blood transfusion, and do not allow her to eat/drink in case surgery is needed.  

Tests include **full blood count, blood group/Rhesus and cross‑match, clotting profile, kidney function/electrolytes, bedside ultrasound for placenta and baby, urine test**, and continuous monitoring of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse and fetal heart rate.  

Treatment is **resuscitation with IV fluids/blood, correction of clotting problems, anti‑D if she is Rhesus negative**, and usually **urgent delivery**—often Caesarean section if the baby is alive or mother is unstable, or induction/vaginal delivery if the baby has died and the mother is stable.  

For now she should **avoid food/drink, alcohol, smoking, herbal drugs, sex, and inserting anything into the vagina**; maintain clean pads/perineal hygiene, wash hands, and after stabilization eat iron‑rich foods like beans, vegetables, meat/fish, and take prescribed iron/folate.

reference: My family member’s child was bitten by a dog. He is a seven-year-old child. When the dog bit him, they usually went to their traditional healer; they made an incision on the wound and applied “apọrọ” (traditional preparation) to it. But now, the place where the dog bit him has started producing pus and it is swollen. We explained to them that they should take him to the hospital. Please, what kind of examination can be done for this boy? Can he have rabies because of the dog, even if the dog itself seems to be fine? And what kind of treatment does this young boy need? Consider that the dog did not cause any further injury to his body.
model_answer:
Take the child to hospital **immediately** because pus and swelling mean the wound is infected, and rabies prevention is time-sensitive.  
The doctor will examine his temperature and general condition, inspect the wound for depth, abscess, dead tissue, tendon/bone/joint involvement, check limb movement/sensation/blood flow and lymph nodes; they may do a **wound swab/culture**, blood tests, and **X-ray** if the bite is deep or near bone/joint.  
Yes, rabies is possible after any dog bite in Nigeria—even if the dog looks normal—though if the dog can be observed and remains healthy for **10 days after the bite**, rabies becomes very unlikely; do **not** wait before starting treatment.  
He needs proper wound washing/irrigation, removal of the traditional substance and dead tissue, possible drainage of pus, antibiotics such as **amoxicillin-clavulanate** (or suitable alternative), pain relief, and **tetanus vaccination/booster** if not up to date.  
For rabies prevention, he should receive **rabies vaccine immediately** and, because this is a bite with broken skin, **rabies immunoglobulin** infiltrated around the wound if available, especially if he has never had rabies vaccination before.

question: Adeolu is a 10-year-old child whose mother was my sister. However, for a few days now, I have noticed that this child sits alone ever since his mother died. model_answer:
Yes, Adeolu’s behaviour can be a normal grief reaction after losing his mother, but refusing food, isolating himself and not talking means he needs close support and assessment.  
At home, keep him with caring familiar people, maintain routine, gently encourage him to talk or draw about his mother, reassure him it is not his fault, allow him to cry, and offer small favourite meals and fluids without forcing him.  
Encourage play gradually with siblings or trusted friends, and inform his school so they can support him.  
Because his eating and withdrawal are significant, he should speak with a mental health professional/child psychologist or counsellor experienced with bereavement; go urgently if he talks about wanting to die, becomes very weak/dehydrated, hears/sees things, or refuses food and drink completely.  
Medication is usually not the first treatment for grief in children and should only be used if a doctor diagnoses depression, severe anxiety, or sleep problems that need it.

model_answer:
Severe lower abdominal pain in pregnancy can be caused by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption/placenta previa, preterm labour, uterine rupture, infection, fibroids, appendicitis, or severe urinary infection—so it must be treated as an emergency.  
Heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is a serious danger sign for both mother and baby because it can cause shock, severe anaemia, baby distress, miscarriage, or stillbirth.  
Warning signs that pregnancy may be in trouble include heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting, fever, bad-smelling discharge, severe headache/blurred vision, swollen face or hands, reduced or no baby movement, leaking water, or convulsions.  
There is no safe “home medicine” to stop such bleeding and pain without first knowing the cause; she needs urgent hospital care with examination, ultrasound, blood tests, IV fluids, possible blood transfusion, and specific treatment depending on the diagnosis.  
For pain, only paracetamol may be used while going to hospital, but she should avoid self-medicating with strong painkillers, herbs, or drugs like ibuprofen/diclofenac unless prescribed by a doctor.

question: A guardian of a child observes that the child is coughing intensely, to the extent that the child is being abrupt and struggling to breathe well. What can cause a child to be coughing in abrupt manner? To the extent that the child cannot breathe well and struggling to breathe. What kind of tests can we run for that child? What treatment can we give? And then what advice can we give to the guardian of this child?
reference: A guardian of a child observed that the child is cough intensely, till the end that the child is been abrupt and struggling to breathe well. What can cause a child to be coughing in abrupt manner, till the end that the child can't breathe well, and struggling to breathe? What can kind of test can we run for that child? What treatment can we give? And then what advice can be give to the guardian of this child?
model_answer:
Abrupt severe coughing with difficulty breathing in a child is an emergency and can be caused by choking/foreign body aspiration, asthma attack, pneumonia/bronchiolitis, croup, whooping cough, or severe allergy/anaphylaxis.  
The child should be assessed urgently with temperature, respiratory rate, chest examination and oxygen level, and tests may include chest X‑ray, full blood count, malaria test if fever, sputum/nasal swab where available, and TB/pertussis tests if cough is prolonged or suggestive.  
Treatment depends on the cause but may include oxygen, nebulized salbutamol for wheeze/asthma, steroids, antibiotics for suspected bacterial pneumonia, adrenaline for anaphylaxis or severe croup, and urgent removal of a foreign body if choking is suspected.  
If the child suddenly started coughing while eating/playing, cannot cry/speak, is turning blue, very weak, or breathing with chest indrawing, take the child to the nearest emergency unit immediately—do not give cough mixtures or force food/drink.  
Advise the guardian to keep the child away from smoke/dust, complete immunizations including pertussis, seek care early for fever/fast breathing, and return urgently if breathing worsens, lips become blue, or the child becomes drowsy.

A dog bite can cause serious wound infection (redness, swelling, pain, pus, fever), tetanus, and rabies—rabies can enter through broken skin from saliva and is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so treatment must start immediately.  

At the hospital, the wound should be washed thoroughly with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes, irrigated with saline, cleaned with povidone-iodine/chlorhexidine, dead tissue removed if needed, and usually left open unless a doctor decides it must be closed.  

Because the dog is unvaccinated/roaming, your child needs rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, plus rabies immunoglobulin injected into and around the wound if the bite broke the skin or bled.  

The child should also receive tetanus protection if not fully up to date, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate are commonly given for dog bites, especially since the wound is already red and swollen; pain relief may also be needed.  

The doctor may check the wound carefully for depth, tendon/nerve injury, foreign bodies or bone involvement, do an X-ray if deep/near a joint or bone, and take a wound swab/culture if there is pus or worsening infection; the dog should be confined and observed for 10 days, but do not wait for observation before starting rabies treatment.

In a 3-year-old who does not respond when called, does not look at people, and seems unaware, the common causes to consider are **hearing impairment/deafness** and **autism spectrum disorder**.

The child should be assessed urgently with a **hearing test/audiology review**, ear examination, and **developmental assessment** by a paediatrician or child development specialist.  

Early diagnosis is important because speech therapy, hearing aids if needed, and developmental support can greatly improve the child’s progress.

A temperature of 38.2°C with shivering after delivery is **postpartum fever**, so do not assume it is only malaria—also check for **heavy bleeding, retained placenta, foul-smelling lochia, uterine tenderness, UTI, breast pain, and high pulse/low BP**.  

If the **malaria RDT is positive**, treat malaria properly with an ACT such as **artemether-lumefantrine for 3 days**; it is safe in breastfeeding, and paracetamol is only for fever/pain, not malaria treatment.  

Give **paracetamol 1 g every 6–8 hours as needed**, maximum **4 g in 24 hours**, after food if possible.  

If fever/shivering continues after paracetamol, temperature reaches **≥38°C again**, she looks weak/confused, has abdominal pain, foul discharge, heavy bleeding, or fast pulse, she needs **urgent review/referral and likely antibiotics for postpartum sepsis**.  

Also encourage fluids, food, breastfeeding, and monitor the baby, but the mother must be reassessed closely today.

question: A 30-year-old woman gave birth a few minutes ago. The delivery was said to be normal. However, since the baby was born, the baby has been having serious difficulty. reference:
A 30-year-old woman gave birth a few minutes ago. The delivery was said to be normal. However, since the baby was born, the baby has been having serious difficulty. The baby is not crying well and is not responding as a newborn should.
After birth, the baby did not cry properly, and seems to have difficulty waking up. The body seems stiff or not moving properly as expected. The baby also cannot feed well and is struggling to breastfeed.
The mother is worried because her previous children used to cry immediately after birth. What can cause this problem? What tests can be done on the baby, and what emergency steps should be taken? What can be done for this newborn baby?
model_answer:
This is a **neonatal emergency** and the commonest cause is **birth asphyxia** (lack of enough oxygen around delivery), but other causes include **infection/sepsis, low blood sugar, prematurity, meconium aspiration, maternal drugs/sedatives, birth trauma, or congenital problems**.  
The baby needs immediate **newborn resuscitation**: keep warm, position the head, clear airway if blocked, dry/stimulate, check breathing and heart rate, give **bag-and-mask ventilation** if not breathing well, oxygen/CPAP if needed, and chest compressions if heart rate is very low.  
Check urgent tests: **Apgar score, temperature, pulse/respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, random blood sugar**, and if available **blood gas/cord pH, full blood count, blood culture/CRP, electrolytes/calcium, chest X-ray**, and later brain assessment if seizures or poor consciousness occur.  
If blood sugar is low, give **IV dextrose**; if sepsis is possible, start **IV antibiotics** such as ampicillin/penicillin plus gentamicin according to local protocol.  
The baby should be transferred urgently to a facility with **SCBU/NICU** for monitoring, oxygen/ventilation support, seizure control if needed, IV fluids/feeding support, and treatment of the underlying cause.

question: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother child, and what kind of care can be given to this child?
reference: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother's child? And what kind of care can be given to this child?
model_answer:
This is most likely a **febrile convulsion (febrile seizure)**—a seizure triggered by high fever in a young child, commonly from infections like **malaria, respiratory infection, ear infection, or sometimes meningitis**.  

During the convulsion, **lay the child on the side**, clear the area to prevent injury, loosen tight clothing, and **do not put anything in the mouth** or force-feed medicine.  

If the shaking lasts more than **5 minutes**, repeats, or the child does not wake up well afterward, take the child **immediately to the nearest hospital/health centre**; health workers may give emergency medicine like **rectal diazepam** and check blood sugar.  

The fever should be treated with **paracetamol**, light clothing, fluids/breastfeeding, and the cause must be investigated—especially **malaria test**, and assessment for serious infection like meningitis.  

Even if the convulsion stops, the child should still be seen by a health worker to confirm the cause and prevent complications.

She should **go immediately to a hospital with maternity/emergency care**, not wait at home or only go for scan, because bleeding plus water and severe abdominal/back pain can endanger both mother and baby.

If baby is still alive and she is in preterm labour/PPROM, treatment may include **admission, antibiotics, steroid injections for baby’s lungs, magnesium sulphate if appropriate, and referral to a centre with neonatal care**.

This is a **medical emergency**: sudden severe headache, stiff neck, photophobia and a widespread rash strongly suggest **acute meningitis with septicaemia**, especially **meningococcal meningitis**, though severe malaria, viral haemorrhagic fevers, and subarachnoid bleeding can sometimes mimic it.  

He should be admitted immediately and treated **before test results** with **IV ceftriaxone** urgently; because he is elderly, many guidelines add **IV ampicillin** to cover Listeria, and give **dexamethasone** before or with the first antibiotic dose if bacterial meningitis is suspected.

If he has confusion, seizures, focal weakness, very high BP, papilloedema, or reduced consciousness, do **CT brain before lumbar puncture**, but **do not delay antibiotics**.  

He should be isolated, monitored closely for shock, and close household contacts may need **meningococcal prophylaxis** such as ciprofloxacin or rifampicin as advised by public health/clinician.

Today, she also noticed that when she is breastfeeding the baby, the baby struggles, gasps, and finds it difficult to breathe properly. She said this is what made her worried because she does not know what is happening to the baby.

model_answer:
Bluish lips in a newborn usually mean **low oxygen in the blood (cyanosis)** and can be caused by serious problems such as **congenital heart disease**, pneumonia/sepsis, airway blockage, aspiration, or severe breathing difficulty.  
Struggling, gasping, or sweating/tiring during breastfeeding can happen when the baby cannot get enough oxygen, commonly from **heart or lung disease**, blocked nose/airway, or infection.  
This is **not something to treat at home with medicine first**; the baby needs **urgent examination today** at a hospital/paediatric emergency unit.  
The baby should have oxygen level checked with a pulse oximeter, chest/heart examination, and may need oxygen, antibiotics, chest X-ray, or echocardiography depending on findings.  
Until seen, keep the baby warm, do not force breastfeeding during gasping, and go immediately to the nearest hospital.

Yes—excessive thirst, passing large volumes of urine often (especially at night), tiredness, blurry vision and weight change are very suggestive of **diabetes mellitus**, especially type 2 diabetes, and he should go to a health facility **as soon as possible** for testing.  
When blood sugar is very high, sugar spills into the urine and “drags” water with it, causing frequent heavy urination; this leads to thirst/dehydration, tiredness, and blurred vision from changes in the eye lens.  
Tests should include **random or fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, urine test for glucose/ketones/protein, kidney function/electrolytes, blood pressure check, lipid profile**, and if very weak/vomiting/confused, urgent assessment for diabetic emergencies.  
High blood pressure alone does not usually cause this pattern, but other possibilities include kidney disease, diabetes insipidus, urinary infection, high calcium, some medicines/diuretics, and excessive alcohol/caffeine—so testing is necessary.  
Until reviewed, he should avoid sugary drinks, energy drinks, excess alcohol, sweets, large portions of refined carbohydrates, drink water as needed, eat more vegetables/beans/whole grains/lean protein, exercise if well enough, and adults should screen for diabetes at least **yearly if at risk** (overweight, family history, hypertension) or immediately when symptoms like these occur.

A 5‑month‑old baby crying with pain in the arms/legs or refusing to move must be brought to hospital promptly, because in Nigeria a common cause is sickle cell “hand-foot syndrome,” but infections in the bone/joint, injury, rickets/vitamin D deficiency, or other serious problems must also be ruled out.  
At home before coming, continue breastfeeding/fluids, keep the baby warm, avoid vigorous massage, and you may give paracetamol 10–15 mg/kg every 6 hours if needed, but do not give strong pain medicines or herbal mixtures.  
The doctor should examine the baby and may request tests such as Hb genotype, full blood count, malaria test, infection markers, calcium/vitamin D tests, and sometimes X‑ray/scan.  
Crawling is not usually expected at 5 months, but severe pain, weakness, swelling of hands/feet, fever, paleness, or poor feeding are danger signs and need urgent care.  
If sickle cell or another condition is found, early treatment and follow-up can reduce pain episodes and help the child achieve normal development.

model_answer:
This is a **neonatal emergency**: a 3‑day‑old baby who is not breastfeeding, very cold, floppy, sleepy, and not moving may have **severe hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, neonatal sepsis**, dehydration, birth injury/asphyxia, or another serious illness—not just “refusal to breastfeed.”  
The baby should be **admitted immediately**, temperature and blood sugar checked at once, warmed safely with **skin‑to‑skin/Kangaroo care or radiant warmer**, and given **urgent glucose support and IV antibiotics** while being assessed.  
Do **not force breastfeeding now**; the mother should express breast milk, and the baby can receive expressed milk by cup/spoon/NG tube only if safe, but if very weak or unconscious, start IV fluids/glucose first to prevent aspiration.  
Routine immunizations should be **deferred temporarily because the baby is severely ill**, and given as soon as the baby is stabilized/recovered; record clearly that vaccines were postponed for medical emergency, not refused.  
This baby should not remain in the immunization queue—move immediately to emergency/newborn care or refer urgently to the nearest facility with neonatal admission capacity.

model_answer:
A cough lasting 2 months with difficulty breathing at night in a 5-year-old is **not normal**, and the commonest cause to consider is **childhood asthma/reactive airway disease**, especially if the cough is worse at night, with wheezing, chest tightness, or triggered by dust, cold, smoke, exercise, or catarrh.  
Other possible causes include **allergies/post-nasal drip**, enlarged adenoids/tonsils causing night breathing problems, persistent chest infection/pneumonia, whooping cough, reflux, inhaled foreign body, or rarely heart problems—even if the TB test is negative.  
Please stop relying on “TB cough medicine” or cough syrups, because they may not treat the cause and can delay proper care.  
Take him to a doctor/paediatrician for examination, oxygen level check, chest listening, and likely tests such as **chest X-ray, full blood count, and asthma assessment/spirometry or trial of inhaler treatment**.  
If he is breathing fast, chest is drawing in, lips look bluish, cannot talk/eat well, or is very weak, go to the emergency unit immediately.

Labour pain itself is normal, but severe continuous pain, heavy bleeding, fever, convulsions, or reduced baby movement are danger signs that need urgent action.

This is **primary postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)** and the common causes are the “4 Ts”: **Tone**—uterus not contracting/uterine atony (most common), **Trauma**—cervical/vaginal/perineal tear or uterine rupture, **Tissue**—retained placenta/clots or rarely a second twin, and **Thrombin**—clotting problem.  
Act as an emergency: **call for help, check vitals, start two wide-bore IV lines, give IV fluids, cross-match blood, empty the bladder, massage the uterus, and examine the placenta and birth canal** for retained tissue or cervical/vaginal tears.  
Give **Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV stat then 20–40 IU in 1 L normal saline/Ringer’s lactate infusion**, plus **Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes within 3 hours of birth**; if still bleeding give **Misoprostol 800–1000 mcg rectally/sublingual**, or **Ergometrine 0.2 mg IM/IV** if she is not hypertensive/pre-eclamptic.  
If the uterus is soft, continue uterine massage and **bimanual compression**; if placenta/tissue is retained do **manual removal/MVA**, and if there is a cervical/vaginal tear, **repair with sutures**—also check abdomen/scan if available to exclude a retained second baby.

What kind of examination can I perform so that I can know what is causing the fever and the inability to turn the child's neck? What kind of result could appear? Within the child's body that could cause the fever and the inability to turn the child's neck.
model_answer:
Titilola, fever with severe shivering and a stiff neck in a child is an emergency—most concerning for **meningitis/brain infection**, severe malaria, or another serious infection, especially since the child can only open one eye.  
Do **not force the neck**; go to the nearest hospital/emergency unit immediately, as the child may need urgent injectable antibiotics/antimalarials and fluids.  
At home you can only check danger signs: high temperature, confusion/drowsiness, vomiting, fits, rash, inability to look down/bend the neck, or worsening eye/face weakness—but these signs mean **urgent hospital care**, not home treatment.  
In hospital, the doctor will examine for **neck stiffness, Kernig/Brudzinski signs, consciousness level, eye/nerve problems**, and do tests such as malaria test, full blood count, blood culture, blood sugar, and possibly **lumbar puncture** if safe.  
Results that can explain this include **bacteria or inflammation in the cerebrospinal fluid**, high white blood cells, low CSF glucose/high protein, positive malaria parasite test, or bloodstream infection.

What could have happened? Could it be that she lost a lot of blood and now needs a blood transfusion, or what should be done for her? Should we give her blood, or should we give her food?
model_answer:
This is an emergency until proven otherwise: postpartum weakness, dizziness and dim/blurry vision soon after delivery may be due to postpartum haemorrhage/shock, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, or high blood pressure/eclampsia—not something to treat with food first.  
Check her immediately: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, level of consciousness, uterine tone, vaginal bleeding/clots, placenta completeness, perineal/cervical tears, and capillary blood glucose.  
Start management at once: call senior help, lay her flat/left lateral, give oxygen if available, insert 2 wide-bore IV cannulas, send blood for PCV/Hb, grouping/crossmatch, and begin IV normal saline/Ringer’s lactate while assessing bleeding.  
If there is heavy bleeding or shock, do uterine massage, give uterotonics such as oxytocin, treat retained placenta/tears, catheterize, and transfuse blood urgently if she is unstable or PCV/Hb is low/significant blood loss is suspected.  
Do not force food now; stabilize her first, and if your facility cannot investigate or transfuse rapidly, refer/transfer urgently with IV fluids, uterotonics, monitoring, and blood arranged if possible.

model_answer:
A baby who is very sleepy and did not cry well 20 minutes after delivery should be treated as **not yet normal until fully assessed**—possible causes include **birth asphyxia/lack of oxygen during delivery, effects of drugs given to the mother (e.g., pethidine/opioids, magnesium), low blood sugar, infection/sepsis, prematurity, or congenital problems**.  
The baby should **not be sent home yet**: check **heart rate, oxygen saturation, tone/reflexes, blood glucose, APGAR history**, keep warm, clear airway if needed, stimulate, give oxygen/CPAP or bag-mask ventilation if breathing/oxygen is poor, give **IV dextrose if sugar is low**, and start antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
At home, the mother should give **only breast milk exclusively** and should **not give water, glucose water, herbs, antibiotics, sedatives, gripe water, or any medicine unless prescribed**.  
If the baby remains sleepy, refuses to suck, breathes fast/with difficulty, develops fever/low temperature, convulsions, blue lips, or yellow eyes/skin early, she must return to hospital immediately.  
The mother should eat normal balanced meals—**rice/tuwo/yam/garri with beans, fish/meat/egg, vegetables, fruits, groundnuts, milk if tolerated, and plenty clean water**—and continue her postnatal drugs/iron as prescribed.

model_answer:
Blue/purple lips in a newborn during breastfeeding usually means **low oxygen (cyanosis)** and, with difficulty breathing or becoming “lifeless,” it is a **serious danger sign requiring emergency hospital care immediately**.  
Common causes include **congenital heart disease**, lung infection/pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration of milk, airway blockage, or prematurity-related breathing problems; **liver disease usually causes yellow eyes/skin (jaundice), not sudden blue lips and breathlessness**.  
Other danger signs to watch for are: poor or no sucking, fast breathing, chest in-drawing, grunting, fever or very cold body, unusual sleepiness/unconsciousness, convulsions, persistent vomiting, severe jaundice, or reduced urine.  
At home, **stop breastfeeding immediately**, keep the baby upright/side-lying, clear obvious mucus gently, keep the baby warm, and **go to the hospital urgently—do not give herbs or force feeds**.  
In hospital, emergency treatment may include **oxygen, suctioning the airway, bag-mask ventilation if not breathing well, checking blood sugar, IV fluids/antibiotics if infection is suspected, and urgent assessment for heart disease with oxygen saturation and echocardiography**.

model_answer:
Heavy vaginal bleeding 6 weeks after the last period could be due to miscarriage/retained products of conception, ectopic pregnancy, fibroids, hormonal abnormal uterine bleeding, infection, cervical/uterine cancer, bleeding disorders, or complications of early pregnancy—so first assume pregnancy-related bleeding until proven otherwise.  
Emergency care is ABC resuscitation: check pulse/BP/level of consciousness, give oxygen if needed, insert 2 wide-bore IV lines, take blood samples, start normal saline/Ringer’s lactate, cross-match blood and transfuse if shocked or very anaemic, and monitor urine output.  
To reduce bleeding while assessing, doctors may give tranexamic acid; if pregnancy loss/retained products are suspected they may give misoprostol or oxytocin and arrange manual vacuum aspiration/D&C if incomplete miscarriage, but if ectopic pregnancy is suspected she needs urgent surgery/gyne review—not blind uterotonics alone.  
If she is not pregnant and it is severe abnormal uterine bleeding, treatment may include high-dose combined oral contraceptive/progestin therapy or IV estrogen where available, plus tranexamic acid and iron/blood transfusion as needed.  
Key investigations are urine/serum pregnancy test, full blood count/PCV, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile, pelvic ultrasound, speculum/bimanual exam, infection tests, and later Pap smear/endometrial sampling if indicated, especially if bleeding is recurrent or she is older.

This is an emergency: heavy bleeding 3 days after delivery with paleness, fever/shivering, cold hands/feet and exhaustion suggests severe postpartum bleeding with possible shock, and possibly infection.  
It is not usually because a “wound was not cleaned”; common causes are retained placenta/tissue, the womb not contracting well, tears in the birth canal, or infection.  
She needs urgent examination now—check blood pressure/pulse, examine the uterus and birth canal, do blood tests/cross-match, and likely give IV fluids, blood transfusion, oxytocin/misoprostol, and antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
If retained tissue or a tear is found, she may need evacuation of the womb or repair, not just injections.  
Please do not delay—this condition can become life-threatening quickly but is treatable in hospital.

This pregnant woman likely has **pre-eclampsia with severe warning symptoms** (high BP plus headache, blurred vision and facial/hand/leg swelling), so she should be **admitted or urgently referred to a facility with obstetric/emergency care**, not just reassured.

model_answer:
Mrs Akinleye, your husband’s symptoms sound like **allergic rhinitis with possible asthma/reactive airway disease**, commonly triggered by **dust, smoke, frying fumes, perfumes, or cold air**—it can happen even in adulthood as the body becomes more sensitive.  
He should see a doctor for examination and tests such as **spirometry/peak flow test before and after salbutamol** to check for asthma, and if available **allergy testing**; sometimes a **chest X-ray** may be needed if symptoms are persistent or unusual.  
Dusty or smoky places can definitely be the trigger, so he should reduce exposure, use a well-fitted mask in dusty areas, improve ventilation when frying, and avoid smoke.  
For treatment, many patients need an **antihistamine** and **steroid nasal spray** for sneezing/nasal allergy, and if he has wheezing or tight chest, an **inhaler such as salbutamol for relief** and possibly a **preventer inhaler** prescribed by a clinician.  
If he is struggling to breathe, has chest pain, blue lips, or cannot speak full sentences, take him to the hospital urgently.
